title: Symmetry and AI-assisted discovery of magic-state factories
authors: Shubham P. Jain, Adam Wills, Shraddha Singh
abstract: Magic-state distillation is a major resource cost in fault-tolerant quantum computing. The cost of a magic-state factory depends strongly on its failure rate, which grows with the number of input magic states. Although symmetry-restricted methods have recently made distance two searches tractable, distance three and above have remained elusive at moderate input counts. We develop symmetry- and AI-assisted methods to search this regime. We present a unified binary-matrix formulation encompassing both triorthogonal-code and direct circuit searches. We show that distance at least three is equivalent to nonzero, pairwise distinct syndromes, separating the choice of syndromes from the search for compatible output gates. We restrict the syndrome search using group symmetry and language-model agents, followed by deterministic solving and independent verification. Our searches yield 699 factory classes, including 564 new ones. These include factories for pure-T states and factories with entangled outputs comprising combinations of T, CS, and CCZ magic states. The pure-T factories [[63, 11, 3]] and [[850, 128, 6]] achieve the lowest overhead exponents we know among protocols with at most 100 and 1000 inputs, respectively, with $γ= 1.589$ and $γ= 1.057$. Our [[1715, 287, 6]] factory, with $γ= 0.998$, is the smallest known pure-T factory with $γ< 1$. We also provide a context directory of search briefs and campaign notes with which readers can train their own agents and tailor the search to their requirements. With these results, we begin constructing an active, open-source repository of magic-state distillation protocols for the quantum community, supplemented by our methods and data, for the practical fault-tolerant quantum computing regime.
summary: This paper presents novel symmetry- and AI-assisted methods to discover highly efficient 'magic-state factories' necessary for fault-tolerant quantum computing. By systematically searching the parameter space, the authors found hundreds of new protocols, achieving record low overhead exponents ($\gamma$) for generating essential non-Clifford quantum states. This effort establishes an open-source resource for the quantum community.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is the resource cost associated with magic-state distillation in fault-tolerant quantum computing, specifically finding protocols for high-distance magic states ($d \ge 3$) at moderate input counts.
main_result: The authors discovered 699 factory classes, including 564 new ones, and reported record-setting protocols, such as a pure-T factory achieving $\gamma = 0.998$, which is the smallest known with $\gamma < 1$.
method: They developed symmetry- and AI-assisted search methods, using a unified binary-matrix formulation, where group symmetry and language-model agents guide the search for compatible output gates.
model_or_system: The context is fault-tolerant quantum computation, focusing on distilling non-Clifford magic states (like T, CS, CCZ) using postselected diagonal CSS protocols. The factories are mathematically represented by binary matrices.
key_observables: The overhead exponent ($\gamma = \log(n/k) / \log d$) is the key figure of merit, alongside the number of factory classes found and the minimum T-count.
important_parameters: The distance ($d$), the number of inputs ($n$), and the number of outputs ($k$) are critical parameters defining the factory structure.
main_assumptions: The search is restricted to the third level of the Clifford hierarchy, and the initial choice of group symmetry ansatz is sometimes heuristic, guided by AI agents.
figures_summary: Figure 1 visualizes the distance-three catalog on the $(n, k)$ plane; other figures show catalogs for higher distances and illustrate specific factory structures as circuits and matrices.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the difficulty of high-distance searches, introducing the unified mathematical framework, detailing the AI-assisted search methodology, presenting the catalog of discovered factories, and concluding with the construction of an open-source repository.
why_interesting: The work directly tackles fundamental resource limitations in quantum computation, providing concrete, optimized protocols that are crucial for scaling up fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

Figure 4 illustrates the ansatz for a representation of the cyclic group C3. Orbits are disjoint and each carries at most one la- bel, so the selected columns have distinct nonzero syn- dromes and thus, by Theorem 1, distance 3 is built-in. The ansatz is therefore a SAT problem. One Boolean variable per candidate slot records whether that slot is selected. There are at most 2kqG variables instead of 2k(2r −1), one at-most-one constraint per orbit, and par- ity constraints on orbit sums for each index Q of the tar- get D.
